description: We are a multidisciplinary team of engineering students (Industrial Electronics, Robotics, Mechanics, and Computer Science) from the University of Malaga (UMA). Team fully assembled.
summary:
Dogtor is a virtual canine companion built for the health and wellbeing of astronauts on space missions. It is designed to collect data from the monitoring systems the crew already uses, such as vital signs and a short daily self-test, and to compare each astronaut with their own personal baseline. In this prototype the data is simulated. Dogtor spots changes early, including fever, space motion sickness, poor sleep, low mood and high glucose, and turns them into gentle, easy-to-follow suggestions instead of extra work.

Findings are ranked in three levels, from a simple suggestion to a true emergency. In a cardiac arrest, Dogtor drops the playful dog, guides the crew through CPR step by step and alerts crewmates automatically.

It matters because on long missions, crews are isolated, far from medical help and under constant psychological strain. Dogtor supports prevention, mental health and fast emergency response in one friendly companion, without adding to anyone’s workload.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Dogtor is a virtual dog that acts as a health and wellbeing companion for astronauts on space missions. Today it works with simulated data, but it is designed so that, in the future, data from the monitoring systems already used in space missions can be configured to arrive in Dogtor and be processed in one place. These include the CSA Bio-Monitor smart shirt (heart rate, ECG, blood pressure, breathing, skin temperature and oxygen saturation), the Actiwatch Spectrum (sleep and activity), commercial wearables such as the Garmin fēnix, Oura Ring and Dexcom G6 (heart rate variability, sleep stages and glucose), and the T-mini sensor (core body temperature). They also include the Tempus Pro portable telemedicine monitor, handheld ultrasound and OCT scanners, onboard blood analyzers, and the EveryWear tablet hub for nutrition, medication, mood and reflex self-tests, with cabin air sensors and radiation dosimeters adding environmental context. Dogtor tracks pulse, blood pressure, temperature, sleep, exercise, diet, glucose and mood, adds a short daily self-test, and compares each astronaut with their own baseline so small changes are noticed early. It explains what it finds in plain language, because astronauts are not doctors, and ranks findings in three levels, from a simple suggestion to an emergency. In a cardiac arrest, the dog disappears, the screen shows step-by-step CPR guidance and the rest of the crew is alerted automatically across devices. The approach is grounded in NASA research.

What benefits does it have?

Dogtor adds no workload ("one task less, not one more"), because in the future it would gather data that is already being measured. It catches problems early, guides the crew in emergencies and eases isolation with a friendly companion. Bringing many sources into one clear view also means the crew sees one simple picture instead of many separate readings.

What is the intended impact?

We want astronauts on long missions, far from medical help, to stay healthier, safer and less alone. The same idea could help on Earth, for people who live far from a city or a doctor, or groups camping in the mountains, who could monitor their health and know what to do in an emergency.

What tools did you use?

The app is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, runs without internet and is designed for a tablet, though we tested it on a monitor. We used AI to generate images and to help with the code. For research and documentation, we used Gemini for fast searches through NASA documentation, and NotebookLM, where we keep a summary of all the documentation we collected.

How is it creative?

The dog as an emotional companion is the core idea: instead of a cold medical dashboard, the astronaut has a friendly presence by their side. A section dedicated to the dog lets astronauts earn bone treats by completing daily challenges and spend them on new accessories, which makes healthy habits feel like a game.

What factors did the team consider?

Our team of six focused on isolation and mental health, the safety of the alerts, and making everything understandable for people who are not doctors. Our main challenges were collecting and processing data from so many different systems and making the results easy to understand.
